title: Swing Rigidity Proved, Fairness Map Settled, and Uniqueness Refuted in Publication Choice
summary: This week settled open problems across game theory and fair division. In cooperative games, Chow's theorem confirmed that a weighted voting game is determined by its swing table. In fair division, all four open implications in a 22-notion fairness map were resolved, alongside new chore allocation bounds. Published uniqueness claims for publication choice equilibria were overturned, and the optimal receiver ratio in bit-string Bayesian persuasion was proved to be 3/2.

fields.name: General Equilibrium & Cooperative Games
fields.context: Chow's theorem proves swing tables determine weighted voting games, and majority veto distortion is at least 5/3.

results.headline: A weighted voting game is uniquely determined by its swing table
results.question: Can two distinct simple games share a swing table if one is a weighted voting game?
results.answer: Every weighted voting game is determined by its swing table among all simple games. The swing-rigidity conjecture is true.
results.why: Settles the swing-rigidity conjecture, proving semivalues see complete structure for weighted games.
results.idea: Chow's parameters are extracted from the swing table, uniquely identifying the weighted game.

results.headline: Banzhaf veto distortion at strict majority is at least 5/3
results.question: What is the worst-case veto distortion of the Banzhaf index under strict majority voting?
results.answer: For quota 1/2 with strict majority, the veto distortion is at least 5/3, improving the known 6/5 bound.
results.why: Sharpens the lower bound on veto distortion under majority quota, while boundedness remains open.
results.idea: Target weights (3/10, 7/10, 0) have optimal weights (1/2, 1/2, 0), giving the first player a veto.

fields.name: Social Choice Theory
fields.context: The Monroe rule satisfies Droop justified representation, while results resolve questions on Droop Monroe, temporal voting, Plackett-Luce entropy, and apportionment.

results.headline: The Monroe rule satisfies Droop justified representation for all instances
results.question: Does the Monroe rule satisfy Droop justified representation when committee size does not divide voter count?
results.answer: Every committee selected by the Monroe rule satisfies Droop justified representation for all n and k.
results.why: Shows Monroe guarantees Droop justified representation unconditionally.
results.idea: An unsatisfied group of over n/(k+1) voters enables a score-increasing candidate swap.

results.headline: Droop Monroe satisfies PJR+ when divisible, but ties break stronger axioms
results.question: Which Droop representation axioms does the Droop Monroe rule satisfy?
results.answer: When k + 1 divides n, Droop Monroe guarantees Droop-PJR+. However, ties can violate Droop-EJR+ and Droop-FJR.
results.why: Settles open entries in classifying Droop representation axioms under tie-breaking.
results.idea: Exchange arguments prove PJR+ when divisible; a three-voter tied instance violates the stronger axioms.

results.headline: Droop fully justified representation does not imply temporal representation axiom BFJR
results.question: Does Droop fully justified representation imply the temporal representation axiom BFJR?
results.answer: Droop-FJR does not imply BFJR in temporal voting, even when no voter approves every candidate in a round.
results.why: Refutes the converse implication, establishing that BFJR is strictly stronger than Droop-FJR.
results.idea: In a four-voter six-round profile, electing candidate 1 always gives Droop-FJR but misses a two-voter BFJR requirement.

results.headline: Plackett-Luce model with geometric weights has linear entropy
results.question: Does the geometric Plackett-Luce model have entropy linear in the number of alternatives?
results.answer: For any parameter φ in (0, 1), the entropy of the geometric Plackett-Luce model is at most C(φ) m.
results.why: Confirms a conjecture from average-case sorting, proving ranking information content scales linearly.
results.idea: Each choice step contributes at most C(φ) entropy; the chain rule sums across all m alternatives.

results.headline: Quota and population monotonicity are incompatible at a common house size
results.question: Can four-state apportionment satisfy quota and population monotonicity at one house size?
results.answer: No four-state apportionment method satisfies quota and avoids population paradoxes at house size 8.
results.why: Eliminates house size variation as a prerequisite for the population paradox.
results.idea: A search over 13,824 quota-compliant assignments across twelve profiles shows a paradox is unavoidable.

fields.name: Mechanism Design & Auctions
fields.context: The optimal persuasion receiver-utility constant is 3/2, alongside negative results for strategic prophet inequalities and forecast pooling.

results.headline: The receiver-utility constant in bit-string persuasion is 3/2
results.question: What is the optimal receiver utility bound under sender-optimal persuasion schemes?
results.answer: The optimal constant is 3/2: receiver utility never exceeds (3/2) R_0, and slice priors approach this ratio.
results.why: Pins down the exact alignment guarantee for bit-string persuasion, settling the open problem.
results.idea: Slice priors achieve ratio (3m+1)/(2m+2), while an extremal lemma bounds the sender.

results.headline: No static threshold is 1/2-robust against strategic reward signaling
results.question: Can a static threshold achieve a 1/2-approximation against strategic reward signaling?
results.answer: In a four-player instance, every static threshold gives at most 721/150 < OPT/2, attaining ratio 450625/930234 ≈ 0.4844.
results.why: Rules out all static thresholds for 1/2-robustness in strategic prophet inequalities.
results.idea: Equilibrium analysis of the signaling game shows reached players distort reports, depressing searcher utility.

results.headline: Sybil-proof and safe procurement exists without winner-take-all outcomes
results.question: Can a Sybil-proof, safe procurement mechanism avoid winner-take-all equilibria?
results.answer: The stake-share mechanism is Sybil-proof, ex-post safe for costs up to L, and admits pure equilibria dividing work.
results.why: Overcomes prior impossibility results by designing a mechanism that shares work without risking insolvency.
results.idea: Agents post costless stakes to split work and rewards; large pools guarantee equilibria with distributed work.

results.headline: Quasi-arithmetic pool score can fail concavity without convex exposure
results.question: Does concavity of the quasi-arithmetic pool score in expert weights hold without convex exposure?
results.answer: Without convex exposure, concavity can fail. For the cubic Tsallis scoring rule with two experts, concavity fails by 23/1024.
results.why: Demonstrates that convex exposure is necessary for concave weight optimization in quasi-arithmetic pooling.
results.idea: Evaluates an explicit forecast pair on three outcomes under the cubic Tsallis rule where concavity fails strictly.

fields.name: Equilibria in Games
fields.context: Counterexamples overturn uniqueness claims for pure equilibria in publication choice.

results.headline: Publication choice problems can admit multiple pure-strategy equilibria
results.question: Does every binary-type publication choice problem with a non-competitive venue have a unique pure equilibrium?
results.answer: A binary-type problem satisfying standing assumptions has three distinct pure equilibria. Three types also yield three equilibria.
results.why: Refutes Theorem 4.1 and Conjecture 4.2 of the paper, overturning claimed equilibrium uniqueness.
results.idea: Equilibrium conditions reduce to roots of a degree-9 polynomial with three valid roots by intermediate values.

fields.name: Fair Division
fields.context: Four open fairness map implications were settled, alongside counterexamples on chore allocations, subsidies, and leximin efficiency.

results.headline: Three open implications in the discrete fairness map are refuted
results.question: In discrete fair division, does MXS imply EEF1, APS imply PROP1, or pairwise MMS imply MMS?
results.answer: MXS does not imply EEF1, APS does not imply PROP1 with unequal entitlements, and pairwise MMS does not imply MMS for submodular valuations.
results.why: Resolves open problems 1, 2, and 4 from the fairness map with small counterexamples.
results.idea: Explicit small instances under additive and partition-matroid valuations separate each pair of fairness criteria.

results.headline: MXS implies PROP1 for submodular valuations
results.question: For agents with submodular valuations and equal entitlements, does MXS imply PROP1?
results.answer: Every MXS allocation is PROP1 for monotone submodular valuations with equal entitlements.
results.why: Resolves open problem 3 from the fairness map affirmatively, extending the result beyond additive values.
results.idea: An EFX certificate with reduced items would force the valuation of all goods strictly below itself.

results.headline: Leximin-optimal EF1 allocations need not be Pareto optimal
results.question: Is an allocation maximizing leximin welfare among EF1 allocations always Pareto optimal?
results.answer: A leximin-optimal EF1 allocation need not be Pareto optimal. An instance with four agents and six goods provides a counterexample.
results.why: Confirms a fair division conjecture, showing leximin selection among EF1 allocations can be Pareto inefficient.
results.idea: The unique leximin EF1 allocation allows a two-agent item swap that strictly improves one agent without hurting others.

results.headline: Envy-free multigraph orientations can need subsidies exceeding n minus 2
results.question: Does subsidy n minus 2 always suffice for envy-free multigraph orientations?
results.answer: Envy-free orientations can need subsidy 3/2 for three agents and 13/5 for four agents. The bound n minus 2 fails.
results.why: Shows the simple-graph subsidy bound fails on multigraphs, narrowing the general gap to n minus 1.
results.idea: Parallel edges force valuations requiring at least 3/2 subsidy across all eight orientations.

results.headline: Connected EF1 allocations and Pareto optimality are incompatible for chores
results.question: Does a connected chore allocation that is EF1 and Pareto optimal always exist?
results.answer: Connected EF1 and Pareto optimality are incompatible for chores: with three agents and five chores on a path, every connected EF1 allocation is dominated.
results.why: Proves that fairness and efficiency cannot be reconciled when chore allocations must be connected on a path.
results.idea: All 12 connected EF1 allocations among the 63 connected candidates are Pareto-dominated.

results.headline: Weighted PROPX and Pareto optimality conflict for chores under unequal shares
results.question: Can weighted PROPX and Pareto optimality hold together for chores under unequal shares?
results.answer: Weighted PROPX and Pareto optimality are incompatible for two agents with chore shares 2/5 and 3/5, 9/20 and 11/20, and 3/7 and 4/7.
results.why: Demonstrates that the conflict between weighted PROPX and Pareto optimality persists even very close to equal shares.
results.idea: Pruned arithmetic verification shows every weighted PROPX allocation is Pareto-dominated.

results.headline: Multigraphs admit PROPm orientations when out-degrees are at most two
results.question: Does every multigraph admit a PROPm orientation?
results.answer: Multigraphs admit PROPm orientations whenever the underlying simple graph has an orientation with out-degrees at most 2, including all multigraphs with at most five agents.
results.why: Proves existence of PROPm orientations for all graphs on up to five agents and low-degree graphs.
results.idea: One agent splits parallel edges into an EFX partition and the neighbour chooses.

results.headline: The cost of EF1 for chores falls strictly below 1 minus 1/n
results.question: Is the worst-case social cost gap of an EF1 chore allocation at least 1 minus 1/n?
results.answer: For two agents, the cost of EF1 lies between 1/6 and 3 minus 2√2 ≈ 0.172. The published lower bound 1 minus 1/n fails.
results.why: Corrects a published theorem, proving that the two-agent chore cost of EF1 is strictly less than 1/2.
results.idea: Shifting chores from the social optimum in cost-ratio order yields EF1 with cost gap at most 3 minus 2√2.

fields.name: Matching & Market Design
fields.context: The Shield-Core upper bound was proved for cyclic Hollow-Shell markets.

results.headline: Hollow-Shell market matchings have at most ⌊(n-1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs
results.question: Can any complete matching in the cyclic Hollow-Shell market exceed ⌊(n-1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs?
results.answer: In the cyclic Hollow-Shell market C_n, every complete matching has at most ⌊(n-1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs.
results.why: Settles the upper half of the Shield-Core conjecture, confirming the exact blocking pair capacity.
results.idea: Cutting the preference circle bounds nested blocking pairs by crossing inversions k(n-1-k) ≤ ⌊(n-1)²/4⌋.

fields.name: Elementary Number Theory
fields.context: A weakly consecutive permutation conjecture was proved for all prime-power lengths.

results.headline: Weakly consecutive sequences of prime-power length begin or end with 1
results.question: Does every weakly consecutive sequence of length k begin or end with 1?
results.answer: Every weakly consecutive permutation of length k begins or ends with 1 whenever k is a prime power.
results.why: Proves Conjecture 5.2 for all prime powers, establishing the first infinite family satisfying the property.
results.idea: Counting residue classes forces both end terms to divide k and be coprime.

fields.name: Combinatorial Games
fields.context: Catch-Up values were machine-checked up to N = 11, confirming published draws and non-draws.

results.headline: Catch-Up draw and non-draw values are machine-checked up to N = 11
results.question: Does Catch-Up on {1, ..., N} end in a draw under optimal play exactly when the sum is even?
results.answer: Catch-Up ends in a draw for N = 3, 4, 7, 8, and 11, and never ends in a draw on odd-sum sets. Lean checks these published results.
results.why: Machine-checks the published minimax computations and parity obstruction for the Catch-Up conjecture up to N = 11.
results.idea: Parity invariants rule out draws for odd sums, while verified pruned search confirms draws for even triangular sums.

glossary.meaning: AnyPrice share: the value an agent can secure against every price vector summing to 1, buying any bundle within its entitlement.
BFJR: a temporal representation axiom, stronger than Droop-FJR
Epistemic EF1: for each agent, the items it does not hold can be redistributed among the others so that the agent is EF1 towards all of them.
Envy-free up to one item: any envy disappears once some single item is removed (a good from the envied bundle, or a chore from the envious agent's own).
Envy-free up to any item: envy disappears whichever single item is removed (any good from the envied bundle, or any chore from the envious agent's own).
Extended justified representation: in a group of ℓ·n/k voters who agree on ℓ candidates, some single member approves at least ℓ committee members.
EJR+: like EJR, but triggered by any unelected candidate the whole group approves, which makes it checkable in polynomial time.
Fully justified representation: a strengthening of EJR to groups that only partly agree, each member approving enough of a common set of candidates.
Maximin share: the best value an agent can guarantee by splitting all items into n bundles and receiving the worst one.
Minimum EFX share: the least value an agent receives in any allocation in which it is EFX towards every other agent.
The optimum: the best value achievable, used as the benchmark.
Proportional justified representation: a group of ℓ·n/k voters who agree on ℓ candidates approves, between its members, at least ℓ committee members.
PJR+: like PJR, but triggered by any unelected candidate the whole group approves, which makes it checkable in polynomial time.
Proportional up to one item: proportionality holds once a single item is added to the agent's bundle (goods) or removed from it (chores).
Proportional up to the maximin item: an agent's bundle, plus the largest of the least valuable items in the other agents' bundles, reaches its proportional share.
Proportional up to any item: for chores, removing any single chore from an agent's bundle brings its cost down to its proportional share.
